questions.stem: A patient after a head injury following a road traffic accident presents with the following symptoms: extreme curiosity, forgetfulness, hyperorality, and increased sex drive. Which of the following structures is most likely to be damaged in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Gray matter around aqueduct of Sylvius

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Amygdala

 

The symptoms described in this patient—hyperorality, increased sex drive, forgetfulness, and extreme curiosity—are characteristic of Klüver-Bucy syndrome, which results from bilateral damage to the amygdala. The amygdala plays a critical role in emotion regulation, memory, and behavioral inhibition.

 

  • Klüver-Bucy syndrome typically involves a set of behaviors including hyperorality (tendency to examine objects by putting them in the mouth), hypersexuality, memory loss, emotional blunting, and extreme curiosity. These symptoms arise due to the disruption of the amygdala's role in controlling emotional and behavioral responses.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Gray matter around aqueduct of Sylvius: This region is related to pain modulation and motor coordination, but damage to this area would not result in the specific behavioral symptoms described in this case.

 

Option C. Lateral nuclei of hypothalamus: The lateral hypothalamus is involved in hunger and thirst regulation. While it is associated with feeding behavior, it does not account for the constellation of symptoms such as hyperorality, increased sexual drive, and memory loss.

 

Option D. Anterior Cingulate gyri: The anterior cingulate gyrus is involved in emotion processing, decision-making, and empathy, but its damage would not specifically produce the combination of hyperorality, hypersexuality, and memory deficits seen in this patient.

 

Educational Objective :

 

The amygdala is most likely damaged in patients with symptoms of Klüver-Bucy syndrome, including hyperorality, hypersexuality, memory deficits, and extreme curiosity, often following a head injury.

questions.stem: How is the muscle spindle able to detect the length while the muscle is contracting?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Nuclear bag fibers

 

Muscle spindles are sensory receptors within muscles that detect changes in muscle length and send signals to the central nervous system to regulate muscle activity. The spindle consists of two types of intrafusal fibers: nuclear bag fibers and nuclear chain fibers.

 

  • Nuclear bag fibers are dynamic and are primarily responsible for detecting changes in muscle length during contraction and movement. They respond to the rate of change in muscle length, making them essential in signaling the central nervous system about ongoing changes during active muscle contraction.
  • Nuclear chain fibers, on the other hand, detect the static or resting length of the muscle. They are less involved in signaling during muscle contraction and are more related to the muscle's position after the movement has stopped.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Nuclear chain fibers: These fibers detect the static (resting) length of the muscle, not the dynamic changes that occur during contraction. Therefore, they are not responsible for detecting length changes during muscle contraction.

 

Option B. Golgi tendon organ: The Golgi tendon organ is responsible for detecting muscle tension, not length. It monitors the force being exerted by the muscle but is not involved in length detection during contraction.

 

Option C. Joint Capsule receptor: Joint capsule receptors provide information about joint position and movement but are not involved in detecting changes in muscle length.

 

Educational Objective :

questions.stem: A 53-year-old male is brought to the emergency department with complaints of right-sided weakness and jargon speech. A CT brain was ordered to rule out hemorrhagic stroke. On neurological examination, there is normal object recognition but loss of comprehension. Which of the following areas is affected?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Superior temporal gyrus

 

The patient exhibits loss of comprehension and jargon speech, which are key signs of Wernicke's aphasia. In Wernicke's aphasia, patients can speak fluently, but their speech lacks meaning, and they have difficulty understanding spoken or written language. This condition is caused by damage to Wernicke's area, located in the superior temporal gyrus (Brodmann area 22) of the dominant hemisphere, typically the left hemisphere.

 

  • Wernicke's area is crucial for language comprehension. When damaged, patients may produce fluent speech that is nonsensical or contains jargon (referred to as "fluent aphasia" or "jargon speech"), but they cannot comprehend language well.
  • Broca's area, located in the inferior frontal gyrus, is involved in motor speech production, and damage to this area causes Broca’s aphasia, where the patient has difficulty producing speech but can understand language. Since this patient has fluent speech, Broca’s area is likely intact.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Inferior frontal gyrus: This is where Broca’s area is located (responsible for motor speech), and it is not involved in comprehension. Damage to this area would cause Broca’s aphasia, characterized by difficulty in speech production, but comprehension would be preserved. This is not the case in this patient.

 

Option C. Arcuate fasciculus: The arcuate fasciculus is a bundle of nerve fibers that connects Wernicke’s area and Broca’s area. Damage to this pathway results in conduction aphasia, characterized by difficulty repeating words, but comprehension and fluency are relatively intact. This doesn’t match the patient's symptoms.

Both A & B: Damage to both the superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke’s area) and the inferior frontal gyrus (Broca’s area) would result in global aphasia, where both comprehension and speech production are severely impaired. The patient in this case has fluent speech, indicating Broca’s area is intact, so this option is incorrect.

 

Educational Objective :

 

The superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke’s area) is responsible for language comprehension, and damage to this area results in fluent aphasia (jargon speech), where comprehension is impaired, but speech production remains fluent.

questions.stem: All of the following can be seen in lower motor neuron lesions, except?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Hyperreflexia

 

Lower motor neuron (LMN) lesions are characterized by damage to the motor neurons that directly innervate skeletal muscles. As a result, the muscles lose their connection to neural control, leading to several hallmark signs and symptoms.

 

However, hyperreflexia is not seen in LMN lesions. Instead, it is a characteristic sign of upper motor neuron (UMN) lesions. In UMN lesions, the loss of inhibitory control from the brain leads to exaggerated reflexes (hyperreflexia) due to the unregulated activity of lower motor neurons.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Flaccidity: Correctly associated with LMN lesions, where muscles lose tone and become flaccid.

 

Option B. Hypotonia: Correctly seen in LMN lesions, where the muscle tone decreases significantly.

 

Option C. Fasciculations: These are common in LMN lesions, as the affected neurons may fire spontaneously, causing muscle twitches.

 

Educational Objective :

 

In lower motor neuron lesions, symptoms such as flaccidity, hypotonia, and fasciculations are common, but hyperreflexia is a feature of upper motor neuron lesions.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man was seen by a neurologist because he had experienced prolonged episodes of tingling and numbness in his right arm. He underwent a neurologic exam to evaluate his sensory nervous system. Which of the following cutaneous mechanoreceptors is correctly paired with the type of stimulus to which it is most apt to respond?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Pacinian corpuscle and rapid vibration

 

Pacinian corpuscles are specialized mechanoreceptors that are responsible for detecting rapid vibration and pressure changes. They are located deep in the dermis and respond primarily to high-frequency vibrations and deep pressure stimuli. When activated, these receptors can provide sensations of vibration or tingling, which is consistent with the patient's symptoms.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Meissner corpuscle and skin stretch: This is incorrect. Meissner corpuscles are mechanoreceptors that are sensitive to light touch and changes in texture but not skin stretch. Ruffini corpuscles are more associated with skin stretch.

 

Option C. Merkel cells and slow vibration: This is incorrect. Merkel cells are mechanoreceptors involved in detecting fine touch and pressure, especially for tasks like two-point discrimination, but they are not associated with slow vibration.

 

Option D. Ruffini corpuscles and sustained pressure: This is incorrect. Ruffini corpuscles respond to sustained pressure and skin stretch, not vibration. They are important in detecting the stretching of the skin but are not involved in rapid vibration.

 

Educational Objective :

 

The Pacinian corpuscles are mechanoreceptors that respond to rapid vibration and pressure changes, making them the correct pairing for detecting tingling and vibratory sensations in the skin.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old male with a pituitary mass causing stalk compression is evaluated for hormonal imbalances. This condition often leads to altered secretion of various pituitary hormones. Which of the following hormones is least likely to have decreased secretion due to sectioning of the pituitary stalk?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Prolactin

 

In the case of pituitary stalk compression, communication between the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland is disrupted. This leads to decreased secretion of most pituitary hormones due to the absence of hypothalamic releasing hormones. However, prolactin secretion behaves differently because it is primarily regulated by dopamine (also known as prolactin-inhibiting hormone/factor (PIH/PIF)) from the hypothalamus, which inhibits prolactin secretion under normal circumstances.

 

When the pituitary stalk is compressed or sectioned, the inhibition from dopamine is removed, leading to an increase in prolactin levels. Therefore, prolactin secretion increases rather than decreases, which is why it is least likely to have decreased secretion in this condition. Patients with pituitary stalk compression may present with symptoms like galactorrhea due to elevated prolactin.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Growth Hormone (GH): The release of GH is controlled by growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) from the hypothalamus. If the pituitary stalk is sectioned, GHRH cannot reach the anterior pituitary, leading to a decrease in GH secretion.

 

Option C. Vasopressin: Also known as antidiuretic hormone (ADH), vasopressin is synthesized in the hypothalamus and transported to the posterior pituitary for release. Stalk sectioning disrupts this transport, leading to decreased vasopressin secretion.

 

Option D. Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH): The release of FSH is stimulated by gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) from the hypothalamus. Without GnRH due to pituitary stalk sectioning, FSH secretion would be decreased.

 

Educational Objective :

 

In pituitary stalk compression, most hormones experience decreased secretion, but prolactin is an exception. Due to the loss of dopamine's inhibitory control, prolactin secretion is increased, making it the least likely hormone to decrease in such conditions.

questions.stem: Platelet derived growth factor acts through which one of the following pathways?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Tyrosine Kinase

 

Platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) acts through the tyrosine kinase signaling pathway. Tyrosine kinase receptors are activated by various growth factors, including PDGF, insulin, and other related factors. When PDGF binds to its receptor, it induces receptor dimerization and autophosphorylation on tyrosine residues, which activates downstream signaling cascades involved in cell growth, survival, and proliferation.

 

The tyrosine kinase pathway is characteristic of many growth factor receptors, making it the correct pathway for PDGF signaling.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. cAMP: The cAMP pathway is often associated with hormone receptors like G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), but it is not the primary pathway for growth factors like PDGF.

 

Option B. cGMP: The cGMP pathway is mainly involved in pathways like smooth muscle relaxation and vision, and it is not associated with PDGF signaling.

 

Option C. IP3/DAG: The IP3/DAG pathway is commonly involved in the action of G-protein-coupled receptors that activate phospholipase C, leading to calcium release and protein kinase C activation. However, this pathway is not associated with PDGF signaling.

 

Educational Objective :

 

Platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) acts through the tyrosine kinase pathway, a common pathway for growth factors that regulate cell growth, proliferation, and survival.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male presents to the physician with a significantly enlarged thyroid gland. Serum T3/T4 levels are decreased. Iodine deficiency is suspected. Which of the following is the function of thyroid peroxidase in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Oxidation of iodide

 

Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) is an enzyme located on the surface of thyroid follicular cells that plays a key role in thyroid hormone synthesis. Its primary function is to catalyze the oxidation of iodide (I⁻) to iodine (I²), which is a crucial step in the formation of thyroid hormones. Once iodide is oxidized, it can be attached to tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin to form monoiodotyrosine (MIT) and diiodotyrosine (DIT), which are precursors to the thyroid hormones T3 (triiodothyronine) and T4 (thyroxine).

 

In the case of iodine deficiency, the thyroid cannot produce sufficient thyroid hormones (T3 and T4), leading to hypothyroidism and, often, an enlarged thyroid (goiter) as the gland attempts to compensate for the deficiency by enlarging.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Na+ iodide uptake: The uptake of iodide into thyroid follicular cells is facilitated by the sodium-iodide symporter (NIS), not thyroid peroxidase (TPO). This is the step before iodide oxidation.

 

Option C. Thyroglobulin synthesis: Thyroglobulin is synthesized in the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) of follicular cells and is not related to the function of TPO. Thyroglobulin provides the scaffold for the iodination of tyrosine residues but is synthesized independently of TPO.

 

Option D. Iodo tyrosine deiodination: Deiodination refers to the removal of iodine atoms from thyroid hormones (T4 and T3) and is performed by deiodinase enzymes, not TPO. Deiodination mainly occurs in peripheral tissues to convert T4 into T3 or reverse T3.

 

Educational Objective :

 

Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) is responsible for the oxidation of iodide to iodine, a critical step in thyroid hormone synthesis. This function is essential for producing thyroid hormones, particularly in conditions of iodine deficiency.

questions.stemHtml: During starvation, the graph of three substances is plotted as shown below. The scale for A and B is on the left, and the scale for C is on the right. Which of the substances are represented by curve B?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) T3

 

In the context of starvation, the thyroid hormones undergo characteristic changes to conserve energy. The graph shows the behavior of thyroid hormones over time during starvation, with three different curves (A, B, and C).

 

  • Curve B represents T3 (triiodothyronine). During starvation, the body reduces the levels of T3, the most active thyroid hormone, as part of an energy-conservation mechanism. This reduction helps slow down the basal metabolic rate (BMR) since T3 is the most metabolically active hormone.
  • Curve A likely represents reverse T3 (RT3), which increases during starvation. RT3 is an inactive form of T3 and rises during energy conservation states to reduce the overall thyroid hormone activity.
  • Curve C represents T4 (thyroxine), which tends to remain relatively stable during starvation. Although T4 levels decrease slightly, they remain higher than T3 since T4 is a precursor that can be converted into either T3 or RT3 depending on the body’s needs.

 

Thus, curve B corresponds to T3, which decreases significantly during starvation, as the body reduces its active thyroid hormone to conserve energy.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. RT3: This is represented by curve A, which shows an increase during starvation, as RT3 is produced to reduce the active effects of T3.

 

Option B. T4: Curve C represents T4, which remains more stable but drops slightly over time during starvation.

 

Option D. DIT (Diiodotyrosine): DIT is a precursor involved in thyroid hormone synthesis but does not fit the pattern of the curves shown in the graph.

 

Educational Objective :

 

During starvation, T3 levels (curve B) drop significantly as part of the body’s mechanism to reduce metabolic activity, while reverse T3 (RT3) increases to further downregulate metabolic processes.

questions.stem: Polyphagia in diabetes is mainly due to:

options.label: A
options.text: Decreased glucose utilization in most of the tissues of the body

options.label: B
options.text: Increased glucose uptake by the whole brain

options.label: C
options.text: Decreased glucose utilization by entire hypothalamus nuclei

options.label: D
options.text: Decreased glucose utilization of VM nucleus of Hypothalamus

questions.answerText: Decreased glucose utilization of VM nucleus of Hypothalamus
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Decreased glucose utilization of VM nucleus of Hypothalamus

 

Polyphagia in diabetes is primarily due to dysfunction in the ventromedial (VM) nucleus of the hypothalamus, which is the satiety center. This center regulates the feeling of fullness and inhibits the hunger center, located in the lateral nucleus of the hypothalamus.

 

  • In diabetes, insulin deficiency leads to decreased glucose uptake in the VM nucleus, as this nucleus relies on GLUT-4 receptors, which are insulin-dependent. Without sufficient insulin, these glucose transporters do not function properly, leading to a reduced glucose supply to the satiety center. As a result, the satiety center is not activated, and the hunger center remains active, leading to persistent hunger, or polyphagia.
  • The inability of the VM nucleus to inhibit the hunger center is what drives the continuous feeling of hunger, even when blood glucose levels are high.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Decreased glucose utilization in most of the tissues of the body: While glucose utilization is impaired in tissues that rely on insulin, this is not directly related to the sensation of hunger. Polyphagia is more specifically linked to hypothalamic glucose sensing.

 

Option B. Increased glucose uptake by the whole brain: This is incorrect because brain glucose uptake is not generally insulin-dependent and does not increase in diabetes. The brain primarily uses GLUT-1 and GLUT-3 transporters, which are insulin-independent.

 

Option C. Decreased glucose utilization by the entire hypothalamus nuclei: This is incorrect. Only the ventromedial nucleus (VM nucleus) is specifically responsible for regulating hunger and satiety through insulin-dependent glucose uptake. Other nuclei in the hypothalamus may have different functions and utilize glucose through insulin-independent pathways.

 

Educational Objective :

 

Polyphagia in diabetes is mainly due to the decreased glucose utilization in the ventromedial nucleus (VM nucleus) of the hypothalamus, which leads to the persistent activation of the hunger center and an unregulated feeling of hunger.

questions.stem: Many signaling pathways involve the generation of inositol trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG). These molecules:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Are derived from PIP2

 

IP3 (inositol trisphosphate) and DAG (diacylglycerol) are second messengers generated in the cell during signal transduction. They are produced by the action of phospholipase C (PLC) on phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2), which is a membrane phospholipid.

 

  • When a signal (such as a hormone or neurotransmitter) binds to a G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR), it activates phospholipase C, which then cleaves PIP2 into IP3 and DAG. These two molecules have different intracellular actions:
    • IP3 stimulates the release of calcium from the endoplasmic or sarcoplasmic reticulum.
    • DAG activates protein kinase C (PKC), which further propagates the signal by phosphorylating various proteins.

 

Thus, IP3 and DAG are derived from PIP2, making option D the correct answer.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Are first messengers: This is incorrect. IP3 and DAG are second messengers, not first messengers. First messengers are external signals such as hormones that bind to receptors and initiate the signal transduction cascade.

 

Option B. Activate phospholipase C: This is incorrect. Phospholipase C is activated upstream in the pathway. IP3 and DAG are produced as a result of phospholipase C activity, not the other way around.

 

Option C. Can activate tyrosine kinase receptors: This is incorrect. Tyrosine kinase receptors are activated by growth factors and other ligands, not by IP3 or DAG. These two molecules are part of different signaling pathways, specifically those involving G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).

 

Educational Objective :

 

IP3 and DAG are key second messengers generated from PIP2 by the action of phospholipase C in response to certain extracellular signals, and they help propagate cellular responses through calcium release and activation of protein kinase C.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old female patient experiencing irregular menstrual cycles and seeking guidance from her healthcare provider. During the visit, the healthcare team explores factors influencing reproductive hormone regulation. Which of the following have a role in controlling the secretion of Prolactin?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Dopamine

 

Prolactin is primarily regulated by dopamine, which acts as prolactin-inhibiting hormone (PIH). Dopamine is secreted by the hypothalamus and inhibits the secretion of prolactin from the anterior pituitary. In conditions where dopamine's inhibitory action is reduced, such as in hypothalamic or pituitary disorders, prolactin levels may increase, potentially leading to symptoms like irregular menstrual cycles or galactorrhea.

 

  • Dopamine suppresses prolactin secretion by binding to D2 receptors on lactotroph cells in the anterior pituitary, preventing the release of prolactin.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Serotonin: While serotonin is involved in many functions within the brain, it does not play a direct role in regulating prolactin secretion.

 

Option B. GABA: GABA is a major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain, but it does not have a direct regulatory role in prolactin secretion.

 

Option C. Somatostatin: Somatostatin inhibits the release of several hormones, such as growth hormone, but it is not directly involved in the regulation of prolactin.

 

Educational Objective :

 

Dopamine acts as a prolactin-inhibiting hormone (PIH) and is the primary regulator of prolactin secretion. Decreased dopamine activity can lead to increased prolactin levels.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is an indirect action of growth hormone?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Anti-lipolysis

 

Growth hormone (GH) exerts its effects through direct actions and indirect actions, primarily mediated by Insulin-like Growth Factor 1 (IGF-1).

 

  • Direct actions of GH include lipolysis, reduction in insulin sensitivity, and sodium retention. These effects are directly caused by the hormone's interaction with its target cells, leading to increased fat breakdown and reduced insulin sensitivity, making GH a diabetogenic hormone.
  • Indirect actions of GH are primarily mediated through IGF-1, which is produced in response to GH. Anti-lipolysis, or the inhibition of fat breakdown, is an indirect action mediated through IGF-1. IGF-1 promotes anabolic processes such as protein synthesis, skeletal growth, and inhibition of fat breakdown in specific tissues, particularly in the liver.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Lipolysis: This is a direct action of growth hormone. GH promotes fat breakdown, leading to the release of fatty acids into the bloodstream.

 

Option B. Reduction in insulin: This refers to the diabetogenic effect of growth hormone, which decreases insulin sensitivity. This is also a direct action of GH.

 

Option D. Na+ retention: GH directly promotes sodium retention in the kidneys, contributing to water balance regulation. This is also a direct action of GH.

 

Educational Objective :

 

The indirect actions of growth hormone are primarily mediated through IGF-1, and anti-lipolysis is one of these indirect effects. Lipolysis, insulin reduction, and sodium retention are direct effects of growth hormone.

questions.stem: "Vasopressin escape" in SIADH results due to:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Downregulation of aquaporin 2 production

 

In SIADH (Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone secretion), there is excess ADH secretion, leading to excessive water reabsorption in the kidneys, which can result in hyponatremia and hypervolemia. However, in the phenomenon known as "vasopressin escape," the body adapts to prolonged ADH action by reducing the effects of ADH on water retention.

 

The downregulation of aquaporin-2 (AQP2) channels in the kidney's collecting ducts plays a critical role in this escape mechanism. Aquaporin-2 is responsible for water reabsorption under the influence of ADH. During vasopressin escape, the body reduces the production and insertion of AQP2 channels into the apical membrane of collecting duct cells, thereby limiting further water reabsorption, despite the continued high levels of ADH. This process helps maintain euvolemia and prevents worsening of fluid overload.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Increase in urine osmolarity: During vasopressin escape, urine osmolarity does not increase but tends to normalize as water reabsorption decreases.

 

Option C. Decrease in ADH secretion: In SIADH, ADH secretion remains elevated, and the escape mechanism occurs despite the high levels of ADH. The body compensates by downregulating the effects of ADH, not by decreasing ADH secretion itself.

 

Option D. Upregulation of aquaporin 2 production: This is incorrect because upregulation of aquaporin-2 would worsen the water retention and SIADH symptoms. In vasopressin escape, there is downregulation of aquaporin-2 to reduce water reabsorption.

 

Educational Objective :

 

In vasopressin escape, the body downregulates aquaporin-2 production and its insertion into the collecting duct membrane, thereby reducing water reabsorption and preventing further fluid overload in patients with SIADH.

questions.stem: Urticaria is seen in a patient. The DLC (Differential Leukocyte Count) that was done will most probably show?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Eosinophilia

 

Urticaria (hives) is often associated with allergic reactions and involves the release of histamine and other mediators that cause vasodilation and increased capillary permeability, leading to the characteristic red, raised welts.

 

  • Eosinophils play a key role in modulating allergic reactions and are involved in preventing excessive allergic responses. In allergic conditions, such as urticaria, the body often increases eosinophil production, leading to eosinophilia. The presence of increased eosinophils is a common finding in blood tests during allergic conditions, including urticaria.

 

While basophils and mast cells are primarily responsible for releasing histamine, which causes the urticaria symptoms, the increase in eosinophils is a response to help control and limit the allergic reaction.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Cytopenia: This refers to a general reduction in blood cell counts and is not associated with urticaria or allergic reactions.

 

Option B. Neutrophilia: This refers to an increase in neutrophils, which is commonly seen in bacterial infections, not allergic reactions like urticaria.

 

Option D. Leukocytosis: While leukocytosis (an overall increase in white blood cells) may occur in some allergic conditions, the specific increase in eosinophils (eosinophilia) is more characteristic of allergic reactions like urticaria.

 

Educational Objective :

 

In patients with urticaria or allergic reactions, the DLC is most likely to show eosinophilia as eosinophils increase in response to help regulate and mitigate the allergic process.

questions.stem: Hypoxia inducible factor 1 alpha stimulates which of the following cells to stimulate bone marrow for RBC production?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Interstitial cells of peritubular capillary

 

Hypoxia Inducible Factor 1 alpha (HIF-1α) is a transcription factor that is activated under low oxygen (hypoxic) conditions. It plays a crucial role in stimulating the production of erythropoietin (EPO), which in turn stimulates the bone marrow to produce more red blood cells (RBCs) to improve oxygen delivery.

 

  • Erythropoietin is primarily produced in the kidneys, specifically by the interstitial cells of the peritubular capillaries in response to hypoxia. HIF-1α increases the transcription of the EPO gene in these cells, leading to enhanced production of erythropoietin, which promotes RBC production in the bone marrow.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Principal cells in the collecting duct: These cells are involved in sodium and water reabsorption in the kidney and are regulated by hormones like aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone (ADH). They are not involved in erythropoietin production.

 

Option B. Type 2 Glomus cells: These cells are found in the carotid body, which senses changes in blood oxygen levels, but they do not produce erythropoietin.

 

Option D. Macula Densa cells: These are specialized cells in the distal tubule of the kidney that function as chemoreceptors, sensing sodium chloride concentration and regulating glomerular filtration rate. They are not involved in erythropoietin production.

 

Educational Objective :

 

Hypoxia Inducible Factor 1 alpha (HIF-1α) stimulates the production of erythropoietin from the interstitial cells of the peritubular capillaries in the kidney, which in turn stimulates the bone marrow for increased RBC production in response to hypoxia.

questions.stemHtml: This is the graph depicting the filterability of dextran through the kidney, with 1 representing complete filtration and 0 representing no filtration. Choose the substance A, B, C respectively. ​​​​​​​
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Polycationic, Neutral, Polyanionic

 

The graph depicts how relative filterability changes based on the effective molecular radius of substances and their charge. In the glomerular filtration barrier, the charge and size of molecules significantly influence their filterability.

 

  • The glomerular basement membrane and the podocytes have a negative charge, which means cationic (positively charged) molecules are filtered more easily, while anionic (negatively charged) molecules are filtered less due to the repulsion by the negatively charged filtration barrier.
  • Substance A (the highest filterability at a given molecular radius) is the polycationic molecule, as it is attracted to the negatively charged glomerular filtration membrane, resulting in higher filtration.
  • Substance B (with intermediate filterability) is the neutral molecule, which is filtered moderately.
  • Substance C (with the lowest filterability) is the polyanionic molecule, as it is repelled by the negatively charged filtration barrier, resulting in much lower filtration.

 

Thus, the correct order is polycationic (A), neutral (B), and polyanionic (C), making option A the correct answer.

 

Educational Objective :

 

In the context of glomerular filtration, cationic (positively charged) molecules are filtered more readily than neutral and anionic (negatively charged) molecules, due to the negative charge of the glomerular filtration barrier.

The net filtration pressure is determined by balancing the hydrostatic and oncotic pressures between the glomerular capillaries and Bowman’s capsule, and in this case, the calculated pressure is 20 mmHg.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old man comes to the physician because of swelling of his legs and feet for 6 months. He has a 40-year history of alcoholism and a 5-year history of hepatic disease. Physical examination shows ascites and edema of the lower extremities. A decrease in which of the following most likely promotes edema formation in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Plasma colloid oncotic pressure

 

In this patient with a history of alcoholism and hepatic disease, the liver's ability to produce plasma proteins (such as albumin) is impaired. Plasma proteins play a crucial role in maintaining plasma colloid oncotic pressure, which is the pressure that keeps fluid inside the capillaries by attracting water.

 

  • In hepatic disease, a decrease in plasma protein production leads to a reduction in plasma colloid oncotic pressure. As a result, fluid is less likely to remain in the capillaries and more likely to leak into the interstitial space, causing edema and ascites, as seen in this patient.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Capillary hydrostatic pressure: This is the force that pushes fluid out of capillaries into tissues. While increased capillary hydrostatic pressure can lead to edema, this is not the primary mechanism in this case.

 

Option B. Filtration coefficient: This relates to the permeability of the capillaries to fluid and solutes. It is not directly related to the cause of edema in this patient’s condition.

 

Option C. Interstitial colloid oncotic pressure: A decrease in interstitial oncotic pressure would actually reduce edema, as it would draw fluid from the interstitial space back into the capillaries.

 

Educational Objective :

 

In patients with hepatic disease, the decrease in plasma colloid oncotic pressure due to impaired protein production (especially albumin) is a key factor promoting edema and ascites formation.

questions.stem: A patient has a creatinine clearance of 100 ml/min, a plasma K+ concentration of 4.0 mmol/L, a urine flow rate of 2.0 ml/min, and a urine K+ concentration of 60 mmol/L. What is his approximate rate of K+ excretion?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) 0.12 mmol/min

 

To calculate the rate of potassium excretion, use the formula:

 

Rate of K+ excretion=Urine K+ concentration×Urine flow rate

 

Where:

 

  • Urine K+ concentration = 60 mmol/L
  • Urine flow rate = 2.0 ml/min

 

First, convert the urine flow rate from ml/min to L/min, since the urine K+ concentration is given in mmol/L:

 

2.0 ml/min=0.002 L/min

 

Now, multiply the urine K+ concentration by the urine flow rate to get the rate of excretion:

 

Rate of K+ excretion=60 mmol/L×0.002 L/min=0.12 mmol/min

 

Thus, the rate of K+ excretion is 0.12 mmol/min, making option A the correct answer.

 

Educational Objective :

 

The rate of excretion of a substance can be calculated by multiplying its concentration in the urine by the urine flow rate. In this case, the patient's potassium excretion rate is 0.12 mmol/min.

questions.stem: In response to an increase in GFR, the proximal tubule and the loop of Henle demonstrate an increase in the rate of Na+ reabsorption. This phenomenon is called? ​​​​​​​
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Glomerulo tubular balance

 

Glomerulo-tubular (G-T) balance refers to the mechanism by which the proximal tubule and the loop of Henle increase their rate of sodium (Na+) reabsorption in response to an increase in the glomerular filtration rate (GFR). This ensures that despite changes in the GFR, a relatively constant proportion of filtered sodium is reabsorbed, helping to prevent excessive loss of sodium and water.

 

  • As GFR increases, more sodium is filtered, and to maintain balance, the tubules increase their sodium reabsorption. This proportional response ensures that changes in GFR do not lead to excessive sodium loss.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Autoregulation: This refers to the kidney's ability to maintain a relatively constant GFR and renal blood flow despite fluctuations in systemic blood pressure. It is primarily involved in maintaining stable GFR but does not directly regulate sodium reabsorption in response to GFR changes.

 

Option  C. Mineralocorticoid escape: This refers to the kidney's ability to prevent sodium overload (and edema) during states of excess aldosterone by adjusting sodium excretion. It is unrelated to the G-T balance mechanism in response to changes in GFR.

 

Option D. Saturation of tubular transport: This occurs when the reabsorption mechanism for a solute (e.g., glucose) reaches its maximum capacity, leading to the excretion of the excess solute. This concept is unrelated to the sodium reabsorption response to GFR changes.

 

Educational Objective :

 

Glomerulo-tubular balance is a mechanism that adjusts sodium reabsorption in proportion to the GFR, ensuring that sodium and water are reabsorbed efficiently to prevent excessive loss when GFR increases.

questions.stemHtml: A patient presents to the emergency department in an unconscious state. An arterial blood analysis was done revealing the values shown. Identify the patient’s condition. ​​​​​​​
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Metabolic acidosis

 

When interpreting arterial blood gas (ABG) results, the first steps involve assessing the pH, pCO2, and HCO3- values:

 

  1. pH: The patient’s pH is 7.250, which is below the normal range (7.35–7.45), indicating acidosis.
  2. pCO2: The pCO2 is 35.3 mmHg, which is on the lower end of the normal range (35–45 mmHg). Since the pCO2 is not elevated, it suggests that the acidosis is not respiratory in origin. In fact, the reduced pCO2 suggests a compensatory respiratory response.
  3. HCO3-: The bicarbonate (HCO3-) is 14.9 mmol/L, which is well below the normal range (22–28 mmol/L). This confirms that the acidosis is metabolic in origin.

 

Given that the bicarbonate is low and the pCO2 is low (compensatory mechanism), the diagnosis is metabolic acidosis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Metabolic alkalosis: This would present with an elevated pH and elevated bicarbonate, which is not the case here.

 

Option C. Respiratory acidosis: This would be indicated by an elevated pCO2 and a low pH, but the pCO2 is not elevated in this case.

 

Option D. Respiratory alkalosis: This would be indicated by an elevated pH and a reduced pCO2, which does not match the patient’s values.

 

Educational Objective :

 

The patient’s unconscious state, combined with a low pH, low bicarbonate, and normal or low pCO2, points to metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation.

questions.stem: Which of the following hormones do not act on the pancreas?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Gastrin

 

This hormone is primarily secreted by G cells in the stomach and acts on parietal cells of the stomach to increase acid production. Gastrin does not act on the pancreas.

 

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. Secretin: Acts on the pancreas to stimulate the release of bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice, which helps neutralize stomach acid in the duodenum.

 

Option C. Cholecystokinin (CCK): Stimulates the pancreas to release digestive enzymes (such as amylases, lipases, and proteases) which aid in digestion.

 

Option D. GIP (Gastric Inhibitory Peptide): Influences the release of insulin from the pancreas and also promotes the release of pancreatic juice.

 

Educational Objective :

 

Gastrin primarily acts on the stomach and not the pancreas, making it the hormone that does not act on the pancreas in this context.

questions.stem: Which of the following hormone is reported to promote the maturation of the hypothalamic gonadal axis during puberty?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Leptin

 

Leptin plays a crucial role in the maturation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis during puberty. It has been shown to initiate the pulsatile release of GnRH (Gonadotropin-releasing hormone) from the hypothalamus. This pulsatile release of GnRH is essential for the onset of puberty, leading to the secretion of FSH (Follicle-stimulating hormone) and LH (Luteinizing hormone), which in turn stimulate the production of sex hormones like testosterone in males and estrogen in females.

 

Leptin levels increase with body fat, and a certain threshold of body fat (and thus leptin) is required to trigger the onset of puberty.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Insulin: While insulin plays a role in metabolic processes, it does not directly initiate the maturation of the hypothalamic gonadal axis during puberty.

 

Option B. Testosterone: Although testosterone is a key hormone during puberty, it is released as a result of the activation of the HPG axis rather than initiating its maturation.

 

Option D. Luteinizing hormone (LH): LH is critical for reproductive function but is released in response to the pulsatile secretion of GnRH, not directly responsible for initiating the maturation of the HPG axis.

 

Educational Objective :

 

Leptin is responsible for initiating the pulsatile release of GnRH, which is necessary for the maturation of the hypothalamic gonadal axis during puberty.

questions.stem: The migrating motor complex (MMC) in humans:

options.label: A
options.text: Occurs only in the small intestine

options.label: B
options.text: Requires an intact intrinsic nervous system for coordinated propagation

options.label: C
options.text: Is the result of food-mediated distension of the small intestine

options.label: D
options.text: Mixes intestinal contents with bile and the digestive enzymes

questions.answerText: Requires an intact intrinsic nervous system for coordinated propagation
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Requires an intact intrinsic nervous system for coordinated propagation

 

The Migrating Motor Complex (MMC) is a cyclic, recurring motility pattern that occurs during the fasting state in humans, specifically between meals, to help clear residual food, secretions, and bacteria from the stomach and intestines. It is often referred to as the "housekeeper" of the gastrointestinal tract because it helps keep the gut clean.

 

  • Requires an intact intrinsic nervous system for coordinated propagation: The MMC is coordinated by the myenteric plexus (Auerbach's plexus), which is part of the intrinsic nervous system of the gut. This system is essential for the proper coordination of gut motility, including the MMC, ensuring the movement of undigested food and debris through the intestines.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Occurs only in the small intestine: This is incorrect. The MMC starts in the stomach and propagates through the small intestine, particularly the terminal ileum.

 

Option C. Is the result of food-mediated distension of the small intestine: This is incorrect because the MMC occurs during the fasting state, not in response to food intake. It helps clear the intestines between meals.

 

Option D. Mixes intestinal contents with bile and digestive enzymes: This is incorrect because the MMC is not primarily a mixing mechanism but rather a cleaning mechanism that sweeps the gastrointestinal tract, preparing it for the next meal.

 

Educational Objective :

 

The Migrating Motor Complex (MMC) is an essential cleaning mechanism of the fasting gastrointestinal tract that relies on the intact intrinsic nervous system, specifically the myenteric plexus, to function properly.

questions.stem: The most common cause of iron deficiency anemia is lack of dietary intake of iron. Iron is transported from the enterocyte to the capillary through:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Ferroportin

 

Iron absorption occurs in the small intestine, specifically in the enterocytes. Once iron is absorbed into the enterocytes, it needs to be transported into the bloodstream. The correct transporter for moving iron from the enterocyte into the capillaries is ferroportin.

 

Ferroportin is the only known iron exporter from cells like enterocytes into the bloodstream. It plays a critical role in regulating iron homeostasis.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. GLUT: This refers to a family of glucose transporters, which are involved in glucose uptake and metabolism, not iron transport.

 

Option B. DMT2: This is incorrect, as DMT1 (not DMT2) is involved in iron transport from the lumen of the intestine into the enterocyte, not into the capillaries.

 

Option D. DMT1: DMT1 (Divalent Metal Transporter 1) is responsible for transporting iron from the lumen of the intestine into the enterocyte, not from the enterocyte into the bloodstream. Therefore, it does not apply to the question of iron transport from enterocyte to capillary.

 

Educational Objective :

 

Ferroportin is responsible for transporting iron from the enterocytes into the capillaries, playing a key role in iron absorption and homeostasis.

questions.stem: The hypothalamus and fat tissues play an important role in the regulation of energy metabolism. Leptin acts by increasing the activity of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Alpha MSH

 

Leptin, produced by adipose (fat) tissue, is an anti-obesity hormone that plays a critical role in regulating energy balance by suppressing hunger. It exerts its effects by modulating the activity of several neuropeptides in the hypothalamus:

 

  • Alpha MSH (Melanocyte-Stimulating Hormone): Leptin increases the activity of Alpha MSH, which promotes satiety (the feeling of fullness). This hormone is involved in reducing food intake.

 

Thus, Leptin increases the activity of Alpha MSH, promoting satiety and decreasing hunger.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. AgRP (Agouti-related protein): Leptin inhibits AgRP, which is a hunger-promoting peptide.

 

Option B. Neuropeptide Y (NPY): Leptin also inhibits NPY, which promotes hunger.

 

Option D. Ghrelin: Leptin inhibits the secretion of ghrelin, a hormone that stimulates appetite.

 

Educational Objective :

 

Leptin increases the activity of Alpha MSH, which promotes satiety and plays a crucial role in energy metabolism and the regulation of food intake.

options.label: B

options.label: C

questions.answerText: CCK from K cell of duodenum and pancreas
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) CCK from K cell of duodenum and pancreas

 

The hormone Cholecystokinin (CCK) is actually secreted by I cells of the duodenum and jejunum, not K cells. Therefore, option C is the incorrect match. The other options are correctly matched.

 

  • CCK from I cells (correct information): CCK is released by I cells of the duodenum and jejunum, not K cells. CCK stimulates the release of digestive enzymes from the pancreas and bile from the gallbladder.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Gastrin from G cells of the stomach: Gastrin is secreted by G cells in the stomach, and it stimulates acid secretion by the stomach's parietal cells.

 

Option B. Motilin from Mo cells of the duodenum and jejunum: Motilin is secreted by Mo cells in the small intestine and stimulates gastrointestinal motility, particularly during fasting (migrating motor complex).

questions.stem: All of the following are true about secretin except:

options.label: A
options.text: It is secreted by S cells of intestine

options.label: B
options.text: It causes release of alkaline pancreatic juice rich in enzymes

options.label: C
options.text: Its action is mediated via intracellular cAMP

questions.answerText: It causes release of alkaline pancreatic juice rich in enzymes
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) It causes release of alkaline pancreatic juice rich in enzymes

 

Secretin is an important hormone secreted by the S cells of the duodenum in response to the arrival of acidic chyme from the stomach. Its primary role is to neutralize the acidic chyme by promoting the secretion of bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice. It also acts via the cAMP signaling pathway.

 

  • It causes release of alkaline pancreatic juice rich in enzymes: This is incorrect. Secretin causes the release of bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice, but it is not rich in enzymes. The enzyme-rich pancreatic juice is stimulated by cholecystokinin (CCK), not secretin.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It is secreted by S cells of intestine: This is true. Secretin is produced by S cells in response to acidic chyme.

 

Option C. Its action is mediated via intracellular cAMP: This is true. Secretin exerts its effects through the cAMP signaling pathway.

 

Option D. It neutralizes the gastric chyme: This is true. Secretin helps neutralize the acidic chyme by promoting the secretion of bicarbonate from the pancreas.

 

Educational Objective :

 

Secretin stimulates the release of bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice to neutralize acidic chyme, but the enzyme-rich secretion is stimulated by cholecystokinin (CCK), not secretin.

questions.stem: In the aftermath of a terrorist attack, humanitarian emergency volunteers handed out isotonic drink solutions containing NaCl and glucose to people with signs of dehydration. These oral rehydration solutions with NaCl and glucose are physiologically more effective than isotonic solutions containing NaCl only. Which of the following is the best explanation? ​​​​​​​

options.label: A
options.text: Primary active glucose transporter at the basolateral intestinal cell membrane facilitates Na+ and water reabsorption from the gut.

options.label: B
options.text: Oral glucose increases insulin secretion, which then facilitates water reabsorption.

options.label: C
options.text: The addition of glucose makes it more likely for the person to drink.

options.label: D
options.text: The cotransport of glucose and Na+ across the apical membrane of intestinal epithelial cells facilitates Na+ and water absorption from the gut.

questions.answerText: The cotransport of glucose and Na+ across the apical membrane of intestinal epithelial cells facilitates Na+ and water absorption from the gut.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) The cotransport of glucose and Na+ across the apical membrane of intestinal epithelial cells facilitates Na+ and water absorption from the gut.

 

Oral rehydration solutions (ORS) containing both NaCl and glucose are more effective in rehydration than NaCl alone because of the sodium-glucose cotransport system in the small intestine. This process is facilitated by SGLT1 (Sodium-Glucose Linked Transporter 1), which is a secondary active transporter found on the apical membrane of intestinal epithelial cells.

 

  • Glucose and Na+ are co-transported together into the enterocyte via SGLT1, and this co-transport enhances the reabsorption of both sodium and water from the gut into the bloodstream. This process is essential during dehydration because it ensures efficient water reabsorption.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Primary active glucose transporter at the basolateral intestinal cell membrane: This is incorrect because the key mechanism for sodium and glucose absorption is via the secondary active transport (SGLT1) at the apical membrane, not primary active transport at the basolateral membrane.

 

Option B. Oral glucose increases insulin secretion, which then facilitates water reabsorption: This is incorrect. Although glucose increases insulin secretion, insulin does not directly affect water reabsorption in the gut during dehydration.

 

Option C. The addition of glucose makes it more likely for the person to drink: This is not relevant in this physiological context. The effectiveness of ORS lies in its ability to enhance sodium and water absorption through the gut, not in encouraging more drinking.

 

Educational Objective :

 

The cotransport of glucose and sodium (via SGLT1) on the apical membrane of intestinal cells enhances sodium and water absorption, making oral rehydration solutions (ORS) containing both NaCl and glucose more effective for treating dehydration.

questions.stem: From which of the following does the tetanic contraction of a skeletal muscle fiber result from a cumulative increase in the intracellular concentration?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Ca++

 

Tetanic contraction of skeletal muscle fibers occurs due to a cumulative increase in intracellular calcium (Ca++). When a muscle fiber is stimulated repeatedly, Ca++ ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum with each action potential. If the muscle is stimulated rapidly enough, the calcium ions don't have time to be re-sequestered, resulting in an increase in intracellular Ca++ concentration, leading to a sustained contraction (tetany).

 

  • Calcium (Ca++) is critical for muscle contraction because it binds to troponin, allowing the interaction of actin and myosin, which produces muscle contraction.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. ATP: While ATP is essential for muscle contraction and relaxation, it does not directly cause tetanic contraction. ATP is required for cross-bridge cycling and detachment.

 

Option C. K+ and Option D. Na+: These ions are involved in generating the action potential and maintaining the membrane potential, but they do not cause tetanic contraction.

 

Educational Objective :

 

Tetanic contraction in skeletal muscle is primarily due to a cumulative increase in intracellular calcium (Ca++), which sustains the contraction by enabling continuous cross-bridge formation.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements are incorrect about vasopressin?

options.label: A
options.text: It's a more powerful vasoconstrictor than angiotensin II.

options.label: B
options.text: Concentration of circulating blood vasopressin after severe hemorrhage can increase enough to attenuate reductions in arterial pressure markedly.

options.label: C
options.text: Uses adenylyl cyclase-cAMP as well as phospholipase C system.

options.label: D
options.text: Secreted by paraventricular nucleus of hypothalamus

questions.answerText: Secreted by paraventricular nucleus of hypothalamus
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Secreted by paraventricular nucleus of hypothalamus

 

Vasopressin (ADH) is secreted by the supraoptic nucleus of the hypothalamus, not the paraventricular nucleus. The paraventricular nucleus primarily secretes oxytocin, which is involved in functions related to love, bonding, and childbirth, earning it the nickname "the love hormone."

 

  • Secreted by paraventricular nucleus of hypothalamus: This is incorrect. Vasopressin is produced primarily by the supraoptic nucleus, while oxytocin is secreted by the paraventricular nucleus.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It's a more powerful vasoconstrictor than angiotensin II: This is correct. Vasopressin is a potent vasoconstrictor, especially in conditions like severe hemorrhage, where it can significantly raise blood pressure.

 

Option B. Concentration of circulating blood vasopressin after severe hemorrhage can increase enough to attenuate reductions in arterial pressure markedly: This is correct. Vasopressin plays a critical role in maintaining blood pressure by constricting blood vessels and increasing water reabsorption, especially during events like hemorrhage.

 

Option C. Uses adenylyl cyclase-cAMP as well as phospholipase C system: This is correct. Vasopressin acts through both cAMP and phospholipase C (IP3/DAG) pathways, depending on the receptor subtype (V1 or V2). V1 receptors are involved in vasoconstriction via the IP3/DAG pathway, while V2 receptors work through the cAMP pathway to regulate water reabsorption.

 

Educational Objective :

 

Vasopressin (ADH) is secreted by the supraoptic nucleus of the hypothalamus and acts as a potent vasoconstrictor and regulator of water reabsorption, while the paraventricular nucleus secretes oxytocin.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man visits his doctor because his wife has long complained of his snoring, but recently observed that his breathing stops for a couple of minutes at a time while he is sleeping. He undergoes polysomnography and ventilatory response testing to ascertain the extent and cause of his sleep apnea. The activity of the central chemoreceptors is stimulated by which of the following? ​​​​​​​

options.label: A
options.text: A decrease in the metabolic rate of the surrounding brain tissue

options.label: B
options.text: A decrease in the PO2 of blood flowing through the brain

options.label: C
options.text: An increase in the PCO2 of blood flowing through the brain

options.label: D
options.text: An increase in the pH of the CSF

questions.answerText: An increase in the PCO2 of blood flowing through the brain
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) An increase in the PCO2 of blood flowing through the brain

 

Central chemoreceptors are primarily sensitive to changes in the concentration of carbon dioxide (PCO2) in the blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). An increase in PCO2 in the blood leads to an increase in H+ concentration (decrease in pH) in the CSF, which directly stimulates the central chemoreceptors located in the medulla.

 

  • An increase in the PCO2 of blood flowing through the brain: This is the correct answer. Increased PCO2 results in more CO2 diffusing into the CSF, where it is converted to H+ ions, thereby lowering the pH and stimulating the central chemoreceptors to increase respiratory drive.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. A decrease in the metabolic rate of the surrounding brain tissue: This would decrease the production of CO2 and thus not stimulate central chemoreceptors. This option is incorrect.

 

Option B. A decrease in the PO2 of blood flowing through the brain: Central chemoreceptors do not directly respond to oxygen levels; instead, peripheral chemoreceptors (e.g., in the carotid bodies) respond to changes in PO2. Therefore, this is incorrect.

 

Option D. An increase in the pH of the CSF: An increase in pH (decreased H+ concentration) would reduce the stimulation of central chemoreceptors. In reality, a decrease in pH (due to increased H+ concentration) activates them. Thus, this option is incorrect.

 

Educational Objective :

 

Central chemoreceptors are primarily activated by an increase in PCO2 in the blood, which leads to increased H+ concentration and decreased pH in the CSF, thereby increasing respiratory drive.

In reality, a decrease in pH (due to increased H+ concentration) activates them. Thus, this option is incorrect. questions.stem: Physical examination of a 41-year-old narcotic abuser reveals an early systolic murmur. The physician also notes a 7 cm distance between the height of the blood in his right internal jugular vein and the sternal angle (normal = 3 cm). Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for the physical findings?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Tricuspid regurgitation

 

The patient's elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP), combined with an early systolic murmur, points toward tricuspid regurgitation.

 

  • Tricuspid regurgitation occurs when the tricuspid valve does not close properly, causing blood to flow back into the right atrium during systole. This results in an increase in right atrial pressure (RAP), which correlates with an elevated JVP. The backflow of blood into the venous system also contributes to the murmur heard during early systole.
  • The 7 cm JVP is significantly higher than the normal range (3-5 cm), further suggesting increased pressure in the right side of the heart.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Mitral stenosis: Mitral stenosis would present with a diastolic murmur, not a systolic one. It typically leads to pulmonary hypertension, not elevated JVP, and would not match the description of the patient's murmur and JVP findings.

 

Option C. Atherosclerosis: Atherosclerosis primarily affects the arteries and does not directly cause tricuspid regurgitation or an elevated JVP. It also wouldn't cause an early systolic murmur or elevated venous pressure.

 

Option D. Aortic regurgitation: Aortic regurgitation presents with a diastolic murmur, as blood leaks back into the left ventricle during diastole. It does not typically affect the JVP or cause an early systolic murmur.

 

Educational Objective :

 

The combination of an early systolic murmur and elevated JVP is most consistent with tricuspid regurgitation, a condition where blood flows back into the right atrium during systole, raising right atrial pressure and the JVP.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic kidney disease presents with elevated serum potassium levels. Despite treatment, the patient remains at risk of hyperkalemia due to impaired renal excretion. The compartment of body fluid Which is primarily responsible for potassium regulation, what percentage does it represent as compared to Extracellular fluid?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Approximately 200%

 

Potassium (K+) regulation primarily occurs in the intracellular fluid (ICF), where the majority of the body's potassium is stored. Intracellular fluid contains about 98% of the total body potassium, making it the main compartment for potassium regulation. The extracellular fluid (ECF) contains only around 2% of the body's total potassium.

 

  • The ICF volume is approximately double that of the ECF. If we consider the ECF as 100%, then the ICF is approximately 200% relative to the ECF in terms of fluid volume and potassium content.
  •    (ICF) (2x) of ECF

 

This makes the ICF the primary compartment for potassium regulation, and it contains about 200% of the volume compared to the ECF.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Approximately 60%: This would underestimate the relative volume of the ICF.

 

Option C. Approximately 20%: This is not correct; the ICF holds significantly more potassium compared to the ECF.

 

Option D. Approximately 5%: This is incorrect, as the ICF holds far more than 5% relative to the ECF.

 

Educational Objective :

 

The intracellular fluid (ICF) is the primary compartment responsible for potassium regulation, and it represents about 200% of the volume compared to the extracellular fluid (ECF).

questions.stem: Countercurrent mechanism is present in which of the following parts of the body? EyeTestesKidneyGutSkin
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 are correct

 

The countercurrent mechanism is a physiological system used in different parts of the body to maintain gradients such as temperature, concentration of solutes, and oxygen exchange. All the listed body parts use countercurrent mechanisms in various ways:

 

  • Eye: The eye utilizes a countercurrent exchange mechanism to regulate the diffusion of gases.
  • Testes: In the testes, countercurrent heat exchange helps regulate temperature, essential for sperm production.
  • Kidney: The kidney uses the countercurrent multiplication system in the loop of Henle to concentrate urine and maintain water and electrolyte balance.
  • Gut: The gastrointestinal system can use countercurrent exchange to aid in nutrient absorption.
  • Skin: In the skin, countercurrent exchange is involved in temperature regulation through heat dissipation.

 

All of these parts utilize countercurrent mechanisms for various physiological purposes.

 

Educational Objective :

 

The countercurrent mechanism is present in the eye, testes, kidney, gut, and skin, making all options in the question correct.

questions.stem: What leads to the detachment of myosin from actin filaments during muscle contraction?

options.label: B
options.text: Cessation of calcium release from sarcoplasm

options.label: D
options.text: Attachment of ATP to myosin head

questions.answerText: Attachment of ATP to myosin head
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Attachment of ATP to myosin head

 

During muscle contraction, the attachment of ATP to the myosin head is responsible for the detachment of myosin from actin filaments. This allows the myosin head to release from the actin, enabling the muscle to relax and the cycle of contraction to continue.

 

  • ATP binds to the myosin head, causing it to detach from the actin filament.
  • After detachment, the ATP is hydrolyzed into ADP and Pi, which "cocks" the myosin head back into position, preparing it for the next cycle of contraction.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Dissociation of ADP and Pi: This dissociation occurs after the power stroke and results in the myosin head returning to its original position; it does not cause detachment from actin.

 

Option B. Cessation of calcium release from sarcoplasm: This is involved in muscle relaxation, but it does not directly lead to the detachment of myosin from actin.

 

Option C. Conformational change in Troponin T: Troponin T binds to tropomyosin and is part of the complex that regulates the binding of myosin to actin, but it is not responsible for the detachment of myosin.

 

Educational Objective :

 

The attachment of ATP to the myosin head leads to its detachment from actin, which is crucial for muscle relaxation and resetting the contractile cycle.

questions.stem: If the membrane potential of this cell is −80 millivolts, the driving force is greatest for which ion?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Ca++

 

The driving force for an ion depends on the difference between the membrane potential and the ion's equilibrium potential. The greater the difference between the two, the greater the driving force for that ion to move across the membrane.

 

  • At a membrane potential of −80 mV, the cell is highly negative. Positively charged ions (like Ca++) are strongly attracted into the cell because of this negative membrane potential.
  • Ca++ has an equilibrium potential around +100 to +130 mV, making the difference between the membrane potential and its equilibrium potential very large. This creates the greatest driving force for calcium to enter the cell.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Cl− is a negatively charged ion and would be repelled by the already negative membrane potential, so its driving force is also minimal in this context.

 

Option C. K+ has an equilibrium potential close to the membrane potential (around −90 mV), so its driving force is much smaller.

 

Option D. Na+ has an equilibrium potential of about +60 mV, which also has a large driving force, but not as significant as Ca++.

 

Educational Objective :

 

The driving force for ion movement depends on the difference between the membrane potential and the ion's equilibrium potential. Calcium (Ca++) experiences the greatest driving force due to its high equilibrium potential and the strong attraction to the negatively charged cell interior at −80 mV.

questions.stem: Fetal hemoglobin has higher affinity for oxygen due to: ​​​​​​​

options.label: D
options.text: Oxygen dissociation curve is shifted to the right

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Reduced 2,3-DPG binding

 

Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) has a higher affinity for oxygen compared to adult hemoglobin (HbA) because it contains two gamma chains (α2γ2) instead of the beta chains found in adult hemoglobin. The gamma chains in HbF bind less effectively to 2,3-DPG (2,3-diphosphoglycerate), a molecule that normally reduces the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen by stabilizing its deoxygenated form. With reduced 2,3-DPG binding, HbF maintains a higher affinity for oxygen, allowing more oxygen to be transferred from maternal blood to the fetus.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Reduced pH: A reduced pH (more acidic conditions) causes the Bohr effect, leading to a rightward shift in the oxygen dissociation curve, decreasing hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen. This is not a factor in the increased oxygen affinity of fetal hemoglobin.

 

Option C. Increased release of carbon dioxide: An increase in carbon dioxide results in increased acidity (via carbonic acid formation), which also shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right, lowering oxygen affinity. This is not the reason for HbF's higher oxygen affinity.

 

Option D. Oxygen dissociation curve is shifted to the right: In fetal hemoglobin, the curve is actually shifted to the left, indicating higher affinity for oxygen, not lower. A rightward shift occurs in conditions that decrease oxygen affinity, such as in adult hemoglobin under acidic or high CO2 conditions.

 

Educational Objective :

 

Fetal hemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen primarily due to reduced 2,3-DPG binding, which allows for better oxygen binding in the fetal environment.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman eats a high carbohydrate meal. Her plasma glucose concentration rises, and this results in increased insulin secretion from the pancreatic islet cells. Glucose-mediated insulin release is mediated through:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) ATP-sensitive K+ channels

 

Glucose-mediated insulin release from pancreatic beta cells occurs via the following mechanism:

 

  1. After a meal, glucose enters the pancreatic beta cells through GLUT2 transporters.
  2. The glucose is metabolized through glycolysis and the citric acid cycle, leading to an increase in ATP levels inside the cell.
  3. The increased ATP/ADP ratio causes ATP-sensitive K+ channels to close, leading to membrane depolarization.
  4. The depolarization opens voltage-gated calcium channels, allowing calcium influx.
  5. The rise in intracellular calcium triggers the exocytosis of insulin-containing granules.

 

Thus, the closure of ATP-sensitive K+ channels is the critical step in glucose-mediated insulin release.  

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. cAMP: While cAMP plays a role in some hormone release pathways, it is not the primary mediator of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.

 

Option C. Carrier modulators: Carrier proteins such as GLUT2 transport glucose into the cells but do not directly mediate insulin release.

 

Option D. Receptor phosphorylation: This mechanism is more relevant for insulin signaling, not the release of insulin from pancreatic beta cells.

 

Educational Objective :

 

Glucose-mediated insulin release is primarily regulated through the closure of ATP-sensitive K+ channels, which triggers a cascade of events leading to insulin secretion.

questions.stem: Different types of neurons evolved with unique properties and their function is related to it. In motor neurons, the site of generation of action potential is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Initial segment

 

In motor neurons, the initial segment is the site where action potentials are generated. This region, located just after the axon hillock, has a high concentration of voltage-gated sodium channels, making it highly sensitive to depolarization. This allows the initial segment to act as the trigger zone for the generation of action potentials.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Axon hillock: The axon hillock is the region where the neuron integrates synaptic inputs, but the initial segment is the specific location where the action potential is first generated.

 

Option C. Cell body: The cell body (soma) processes incoming signals but does not typically generate action potentials.

 

Option D. First Node of Ranvier: In sensory neurons, the first node of Ranvier is the site of action potential initiation, but in motor neurons, it occurs at the initial segment.

 

Educational Objective :

 

In motor neurons, action potentials are generated at the initial segment, which is the most sensitive region for initiating these signals due to the high density of voltage-gated sodium channels.

questions.stem: Which among the following has the highest airway resistance?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Bronchi

 

The bronchi have the highest airway resistance in the respiratory tract. Airway resistance is determined by the radius of the airways, and the larger bronchi, despite having a wider diameter than smaller airways, contribute the most to resistance due to their reduced total cross-sectional area compared to smaller airways like the bronchioles and alveolar ducts.

 

As you move down the respiratory tree, the number of airways increases significantly, which compensates for their smaller individual diameters, resulting in lower overall resistance in the smaller airways, including the small bronchioles and respiratory bronchioles.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Alveolar duct: The alveolar ducts are very small and have low resistance due to their large combined surface area and low airflow velocity at that level.

 

Option C. Respiratory bronchioles: These airways are smaller than bronchi, but because of their large number and cumulative cross-sectional area, they contribute less to total airway resistance.

 

Option D. Small bronchioles: Although they are narrow, their cumulative cross-sectional area is large, reducing overall airway resistance.

 

Educational Objective :

 

The bronchi contribute the most to airway resistance due to their smaller total cross-sectional area compared to smaller airways, despite having a larger individual diameter.

questions.stem: All of the following ions have maximum reduction in their concentration on the luminal side of proximal convoluted tubule except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Chloride

 

In the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT), the majority of substances are reabsorbed, resulting in a significant reduction of their concentration in the lumen. However, the degree of reabsorption varies.

 

  • Chloride: Around 60% of chloride is reabsorbed in the PCT, leaving about 40% of its original concentration still in the lumen. Thus, it does not experience the same degree of reduction in concentration as glucose or amino acids.

 

Therefore, chloride has the least reduction in its concentration in the lumen compared to the other options, making it the correct answer.

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Amino acids: Almost completely reabsorbed in the PCT, leaving virtually none in the lumen.

 

Option B. Glucose: Completely reabsorbed in healthy individuals, leaving none in the lumen.

 

Option D. Bicarbonate: About 85% reabsorbed, but not as high as glucose or amino acids.

 

Educational Objective :

 

While most ions are reabsorbed in the PCT, chloride experiences the least reduction in concentration compared to glucose, amino acids, and bicarbonate.

Educational Objective : While most ions are reabsorbed in the PCT, chloride experiences the least reduction in concentration compared to glucose, amino acids, and bicarbonate.

questions.stem: The sodium iodide symporter is present in all of the following except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Pituitary gland

 

The sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) is a membrane protein that facilitates the active transport of iodide into cells, primarily involved in iodine uptake for the production of thyroid hormones. It is present in several tissues involved in iodide metabolism:

 

  • Pituitary gland: The pituitary gland does not contain the NIS. It plays a role in regulating thyroid function through the secretion of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) but does not directly participate in iodide transport or concentration.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Thyroid gland: The NIS is critical for iodide uptake in thyroid hormone production.

 

Option B. Placenta: It helps transfer iodide from the maternal circulation to the fetus.

 

Option C. Salivary gland: It contributes to iodide homeostasis.

 

Educational Objective :

 

The sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) is primarily involved in tissues related to iodide uptake for thyroid hormone synthesis, but it is not found in the pituitary gland, which regulates thyroid function through hormone release rather than direct iodide transport.
